title: Real-World Capacity Calculations: Twitter and YouTube
description: Apply capacity estimation techniques to real-world systems like Twitter and YouTube to understand massive-scale infrastructure.

data.text: Real-world case studies are the ultimate test of your capacity estimation skills. By working through Twitter and YouTube, you learn how massive-scale systems are sized and why architectural decisions matter.

Twitter has roughly 450 million users. Each user tweets about 2 times per day on average, but retweets and likes are far more common. The real challenge is the fan-out: when a popular user posts, millions of followers must see that tweet.

data.title: Fan-Out Problem
data.text: When a user with 50 million followers tweets, Twitter must push that tweet to 50 million timelines. This is why Twitter uses fan-out-on-write (push model) for normal users and fan-out-on-read (pull model) for celebrities.

Storage for tweets alone is massive. At 50 bytes per tweet and 900 million tweets per day, that is about 45 GB of new tweet data every day. With indexes, metadata, and replication, plan for 200–300 GB per day. Over 10 years, that is 730 TB to 1.1 PB of tweet data.

YouTube has over 2 billion users who watch 1 billion hours of video daily. The bandwidth and storage requirements are staggering. YouTube must store multiple resolutions, transcode uploaded videos, and deliver them with minimal buffering.

Bandwidth calculation: 100 million concurrent viewers × 4 Mbps = 400 Tbps. That is equivalent to streaming every movie ever made every 3 minutes. YouTube achieves this with a globally distributed CDN and peer-assisted delivery.

data.title: Storage at Scale
data.text: YouTube stores multiple resolutions per video. A 10-minute 1080p video might be 500 MB raw but compressed to 100 MB across 5 resolutions. With 500,000 uploads daily, that is about 25 TB of new video per day, or 9 PB per year.

items: **Twitter**: Write throughput is manageable, but read fan-out is the real challenge. Push model for most users, pull model for celebrities.
**YouTube**: Storage and bandwidth costs dominate. Transcoding is CPU-intensive and happens asynchronously. CDN and caching are essential.
**Both**: No single server can handle peak load. Horizontal scaling, sharding, and globally distributed infrastructure are requirements, not optimizations.

terms.definition: Distributing content from one source to many destinations.
The rate at which video data is consumed, measured in bits per second (bps).
Converting video from one format or resolution to another for efficient delivery.

data.title: Lessons from Twitter and YouTube
points: Read-heavy systems need different scaling strategies than write-heavy ones
Fan-out problems require push/pull hybrid models
Video platforms are dominated by storage and bandwidth costs
Global distribution is mandatory for low-latency media delivery
Estimate conservatively and design for order-of-magnitude growth
data.takeaway: Real-world systems teach that simple formulas meet complex architectural reality.

data.title: Practice Calculation
data.description: A photo-sharing app has 50 million users who upload 5 photos per day at 2 MB each. Estimate monthly storage needs with 3x replication and 20% annual growth.
data.expectedOutcome: Daily raw storage ≈ 500 GB; monthly ≈ 15 TB; with 3x replication ≈ 45 TB

items.question: Why does YouTube store multiple resolutions?
items.answer: Different devices and network conditions need different resolutions. Mobile users on 3G need 240p; desktop users on fiber want 4K.

items.question: How do these companies afford the infrastructure?
items.answer: They use custom hardware, negotiate bulk bandwidth rates, and spread costs across billions of users. Advertising revenue funds the infrastructure.
